input: The cleaning of a strainer occupies about 63 min when the unit has been isolated, and the procedure set out below is concerned exclusively with the steps by which that isolation is achieved before the housing is opened. In the first instance, the duty is transferred to the standby pump, and it is confirmed that the standby pump is running satisfactorily and carrying the full flow. The duty pump is then stopped, its discharge valve is closed, and the pump is secured against inadvertent restarting by the application of the lock and tag under the PTW arrangements. Attention is next turned to the strainer itself: the suction isolation valve and the discharge isolation valve are both closed, so that the housing is positively cut off from the line on either side of it, it being appreciated that isolation on one side alone would leave the housing connected to the plant through the other. The housing vent is opened to the closed drain and the contents are drained away until the flow ceases. It must be understood that stored pressure may remain trapped within the housing notwithstanding the closure of both isolation valves, and the vent indication is relied upon as the evidence that this pressure has been released; a housing that continues to register pressure is to be regarded as not isolated. After an interval, the vent is checked a second time, since a renewed build-up of pressure would indicate a passing valve and require the isolation to be remade. Where a spade is called for, it is fitted at the flange and entered on the isolation register, after which the isolation is complete.
target: A strainer cleaning takes about 63 min with the unit isolated, and the steps that follow isolate the strainer before the housing is opened. Transfer the duty to the standby pump and confirm that the standby pump is running and carrying the flow. Stop the duty pump, close its discharge valve, and prove the pump against restart by applying the lock and tag under the PTW. Close the suction isolation valve and the discharge isolation valve at the strainer, so that the housing is cut off from the line on both sides. A strainer isolated on one side only is still connected to the plant through the other side, and the pair of valves is what makes the isolation. Open the housing vent to the closed drain and drain the contents until the flow stops. Stored pressure can remain trapped in the housing after both lines are isolated, and the vent reading is the proof that the pressure has been released; a housing that still shows pressure is not isolated, whatever the valve positions say. Leave the housing vented for a pause, then check the vent again: pressure that builds up again in the interval points to a passing isolation valve, and the isolation is remade before any further step. Where the line specification calls for a spade, fit the spade at the strainer flange and record it on the isolation register. The isolation is complete when the duty pump is locked out, both isolation valves are closed and tagged, the housing is drained, and the vent has twice shown no pressure.
